## Process lifecycle

- Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
- Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
- After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

## Linux browser and WebGPU capture

- Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
- Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
- Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
- Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
- Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
- Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
- Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
- Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
- Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

## Mobile browser games

- Support Android and iOS phones and tablets with responsive layouts and usable touch controls.
- Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
- Add tilt controls only when appropriate; offer touch alternatives and request iOS motion permission from a user gesture when needed.
- Follow explicit device and control requirements in the user request.

# OMG (Oh My GitHub) agent instructions

Do not implement, suggest, report, or propose security issues unless the user explicitly asks for a security review.
Inspect the OpenCode implementation at `/Users/igor/Documents/ChatGPT/opencode` and [anomalyco/opencode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) for related requests.

## Wiki index

- [OpenCode workflow](wiki/opencode.md)
- [Test OpenCode execution](wiki/opencode-v2-experiment.md)
- [Oh My Github App](https://github.com/denaidark/omsite/blob/main/wiki/oh-my-github-app.md)
- [Temporary Mac SSH access](wiki/access.md)
- [Testing and verification](wiki/testing.md)
- [OmGithub publishing](https://github.com/denaidark/omsite/blob/main/wiki/omgithub.md)


## Main project file

The main project file is [.github/workflows/opencode.yml](.github/workflows/opencode.yml).

Keep the local [game issue E2E skill](.agents/skills/game-issue-e2e/SKILL.md)
aligned with this workflow. Create an issue with `OpenCode` and only user-requested mode labels already attached, to start the native `issues.opened` listener. Wait only for the
initial OpenCode session link during E2E kickoff. Install the listener on the
default branch before requesting execution. Validate author access and freeze
the request inside Actions before starting the reusable execution job.
Set repository variable `OPENCODE_ACCESS=everyone` to accept any issue author
for labeled issues. Keep the App as a setup
helper. Use Actions concurrency to serialize each issue.
Store `branch` in an `omgithub-request:v1` JSON HTML comment to select the
project checkout, result base, and workflow. Let default-branch preparation
dispatch the selected branch. Run preparation and OpenCode in that branch run.

## Shell timing

When writing shell scripts,
always add explicit per-command execution-time measurements between commands.
Use `/usr/bin/time -p` or a small timing helper around each meaningful command;
the outer command duration is not sufficient because it hides which step is
slow or hung. Use `/usr/bin/time` only in scripts; do not invoke it directly in
interactive shell commands.

## Ideas

Store durable implementation ideas as individual Markdown files under
`./ideas/`, using descriptive kebab-case filenames such as
`ideas/opencode-oauth-env-auth.md`.




## Links in handoffs

When a relevant URL or stable identifier exists, include a clickable Markdown
link in the user-facing response. Link GitHub issues, Actions runs, pull
requests, commits, releases, public app URLs, and Codex tasks/threads rather
than reporting only their numbers or plain text. For Codex tasks/threads, use
the `codex://threads/<thread-id>` URL format.

When mentioning a commit, append its relative age in hours or days.

## OpenCode GitHub Actions

To execute an issue, create it with `OpenCode` and only mode labels explicitly requested by the user.
Check for a native `issues` run and successful preparation.
The workflow starts a temporary AgentsWeb SSH session,
verifies it, runs OpenCode, and cleans up the SSH session afterward.

When monitoring a triggered run, use `gh run watch <run-id> --repo denaidark/OhMyGithub --exit-status` for overall job status.
Do not use `gh run view --log` to read logs from a running task: GitHub reports that
logs are unavailable until completion. Use `bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id>`
for the live Actions log over SSH. Do not use tight `for` loops around `gh run list`,
which needlessly consume GitHub API rate limit.

Free OpenCode models are limited per egress IP, not per account.
Treat a local `FreeUsageLimitError` 429 as local only.
Read the runner's own `Selected model` and provider errors before blaming quota.
Use `retryAfterMs` as the reset bound.
Run repeated V2 tests with a connected provider; do not spend the free allowance on retries.

Interrupting a V2 turn before the assistant message projects leaves no stopped message to save.
Wait for that assistant message before requiring the interrupted idle marker.

To connect to an issue's live worker, find its run ID with
`gh run list --repo denaidark/OhMyGithub --workflow opencode.yml --status in_progress`,
then run `bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id>` to discover the host and port and SSH
with `~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb` as shown by the helper.

When the user asks to check a live OpenCode workflow, always pull the runner logs
over SSH first, using `scripts/ssh-run-log.sh` or a targeted SSH read from the
same runner. Base the answer on those logs before discussing whether an action
is confirmed; do not lead with a generic inability-to-confirm statement when
live log evidence can be collected.

For real-time inspection from a live temporary SSH session, use the helper:

```sh
bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id>
```

The helper discovers the temporary SSH command from the triggering issue or pull
request, then follows the freshest `_diag/pages` log. The runner uploads chunks from
`_diag/blocks` to GitHub. Do not print environment files, tokens, or private keys while
inspecting the runner.

The Mac private key stays at `~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb`. Its public key is

```

The command works only while the corresponding Actions job is running.

# Testing and verification

## Use the preconfigured Linux CLI

Run `scripts/setup-linux-playwright.sh` on an Ubuntu worker to install the pinned
CLI, Chromium, Mesa Vulkan drivers, and a persistent Xvfb display. Let the reusable
workflow run this before publishing SSH access. Use `playwright-cli` from Actions
or a fresh SSH shell; let the wrapper supply DISPLAY and the Linux configuration.
Use `playwright-cli -s=check open <url>`, `eval`, `screenshot`, and `close` without
manual browser flags. Load `.github/templates/linux.md` by default. Select `mac.md` instead when
a `mac` label or `#mac` hashtag is present. Match case insensitively. Recheck the actual screenshot after upgrades.

## Capture the Linux WebGPU triangle

Install Playwright 1.63.0 and its full Chromium browser as below. Install
`mesa-vulkan-drivers`, `vulkan-tools`, and `xvfb` on Ubuntu. Serve
`tests/fixtures/webgpu-triangle.html` over localhost HTTP. Run:

```sh
PLAYWRIGHT_ROOT=/tmp/gpu-runtime xvfb-run -a node scripts/gpu-capture.mjs \
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/webgpu-triangle.html --canvas '#wgpu' \
  --backend swiftshader --require-green-triangle --out /tmp/linux-triangle
```

Require green triangle pixels, a usable device, `scene.webgpu.rendered=true`,
and no page errors. Inspect the image. Treat SwiftShader and Mesa llvmpipe as
CPU rendering, not GPU hardware acceleration. Use the headed Xvfb result on
[run 34908797646](https://github.com/AgentsLoop/PlayGround/actions/runs/34908797646)
as the verified 2026-09-15 reference. Do not accept the headless result from
that run: its initial generic pixel check falsely accepted background pixels.
Retain the fixture's GPU reference. Preserve failed diagnostics when investigating
`A valid external Instance reference no longer exists`. Do not infer a single
root cause from the combined driver-installation and fixture changes.
Use `--backend vulkan` for native-driver experiments, `--backend swangle` for
ANGLE SwiftShader experiments, and `--executable` to select another browser.
Keep the default Metal path for the Mac test.

## Capture Pascal Editor on Linux

Use `http://localhost:3002`, not the numeric loopback origin, with the default
Pascal Next.js development server. Check the server log for blocked development
resources when HTTP 403 or HMR handshake errors occur.
Install dependencies with the repository's Bun lockfile. Start `bun dev` and
wait for the editor on port 3002. Create a studio through `POST /api/scenes`
using the documented scene structure. Open `/scene/<id>?disable=postFx` for
the reduced-effects capture. Do not use the empty root page as a scene test.
Run headed Chromium under Xvfb with the tested SwiftShader flags above.
Wait for visible geometry; verify the existing canvas accepts `webgpu` and
rejects `webgl2`. Require the viewer's `WebGPU device ready` log, no failed
HTTP requests, and no JavaScript errors. Inspect the screenshot manually.
Treat the 2026-09-15 room capture on issue 113 as a software-rendering result.
Do not claim full post-processing coverage. Preserve readiness-timeout warnings
in the report; do not confuse an earlier WebGL fallback capture with the final
WebGPU capture. Keep the saved scene and application server for further tests.

## Capture WebGPU on a hosted Mac

Use full Chromium with the Metal backend. Keep Playwright's other launch defaults. Test
headed mode first; use `--headless` only after comparing the actual captures.
Install Playwright and its full Chromium build in a separate runtime directory:

```sh
npm install --prefix /tmp/gpu-capture-runtime playwright@1.63.0
/tmp/gpu-capture-runtime/node_modules/.bin/playwright install chromium
PLAYWRIGHT_ROOT=/tmp/gpu-capture-runtime node scripts/gpu-capture.mjs \
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/ --canvas '#wgpu' \
  --require-metal --out /tmp/game-capture
```

Replace the URL and canvas selector with the running game's values. Start the
game before capture if it requires user input. Read `diagnostic.json`,
`canvas.png`, and `page.png` from the output directory. Require an available
WebGPU device, no page errors, and painted canvas pixels. Exclude CSS borders
from the pixel check. Accept a flat triangle with two interior colours; reject
a uniform interior even when its border has another colour.

Use `--baseline` to test full Chromium without extra flags. Use `--headless`
to test the same full browser headlessly. Do not substitute the separate
headless shell. Preserve failed diagnostics; do not silently skip absent
adapters. Keep Vulkan flags out of the macOS Metal capture path.

Use the verified flags: `--enable-gpu`, `--ignore-gpu-blocklist`,
`--enable-unsafe-webgpu`, and `--use-angle=metal`. Check `chrome://gpu` in a
separate headed page. Interpret `Apple Paravirtual device` as a virtual Metal
adapter, not proof of a physical GPU model or hardware performance.

Refer to [Playwright's browser documentation](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#opt-in-to-new-headless-mode)

- "smile": huge teeth grin, unmoving, eyes don't blink
- "hat": human has hats too; not a tell.
Also combo.
All anomalies should have at least one "strong" tell (tall, extra arms, extra eyes, no face, backwards, float, duplicate) so it's fair. Weaker tells (skin, fingers, twitch) can accompany.

Human models: skin tones, hair colors/styles, shirts, pants, hats, glasses, mustache, height 0.9-1.1, some fat. Faces: draw with canvas: eyes, brows, mouth, maybe blush. All facing camera. A couple of humans can be "weird but human" (e.g., clown, goth) to test. Maybe a human on stilts? No, unfair.

The player needs to distinguish at a glance. With low-poly, extra arms and eyes are visible. Tells should be big enough.

Count: group size 1-3 for humans. Display "3 PEOPLE" maybe. Subtitle lines from one of them. If group accepted, all walk in. Group members each count. Humans groups add party. Each knock, choose anomaly with probability that ramps: maybe 0.28 early, 0.42 later. Since anomalies don't reduce needed count, you may see many. Need 50 guests; expected humans per round 2; need ~25 human rounds; with 35% anomalies, ~38 rounds. That's long. Use groups 2-4 → avg 3; ~17 human rounds, 26 total. Better. But peeping at 3 people at once is harder; that's fun. Let's do groups 1-3, avg 2.2; and "50 guests" but humans can bring +1 each? Hmm.

Alternative: guest counter counts "humans" but each accepted group gives a random 2-6. Let's do groups 2-4 (avg 3) and anomalies 30%: ~17 human knocks + 7 anomalies = 24 doors. That's about right.

Maybe accept groups of 1-3 but each group fills count by group size; and require 30 instead of 50? User explicitly says 50. Keep 50. Make group size 2-5 with humor ("a group of 4"). Avg 3.2, 16 human rounds, 6 anomalies. 22 rounds. Good. However, peeping 5 figures is visually crowded and any anomaly tell needs to be spotted. But anomalies are solo, so no mixed groups. That's manageable.

Wait, "with 50 humans you do an house party" — if the player rejects humans, count doesn't advance, so no fail. To create stakes, maybe rejected humans get angry and can cause a "bad review" meter? Not needed; failure only via anomaly. But could add "PATIENCE" meter: if you keep rejecting humans, the party never happens; there's no fail. Fine — it's a "bad quality" game, the tension is the anomaly.

Maybe add a shift timer? No, keep it relaxed.

Visual progression details:
- Guests physically spawn in the room. With 50 guests, low-poly crowd might be heavy but fine (50 × ~10 meshes = 500 draw calls, at low res okay). Use shared geometries/materials, faces unique textures. Could use InstancedMesh but each face unique; simpler groups. 50 people × maybe 8 meshes = 400 draw calls; likely fine. Reduce by merging body pieces? For party, spawn simple "party people" with 4 meshes (body, head, 2 arms). We'll build visitor models with ~10 meshes. 50*10=500. Acceptable on desktop; on mobile maybe 30fps. Can cap visible guests at 50 with simple models.

- Decoration spawns: balloons at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; banner at 50; chips/drinks; disco ball maybe. Party lights (colored point lights) at 50; before that warm lights.

- The room can be seen when looking back from the door. So guests visible. Good.

- The camera at the door: you can look around 360, but movement locked. Actually after the letter, the player is auto-placed 1.2m from door facing it. Mouse look allowed with yaw ±? Allow full 360 to see party. In peephole, camera moves outside, and on step back returns.

- During party at 50, maybe unlock movement so player can walk into the party? But then the final knock. We could auto-play a cutscene: camera turns around to view party, guests dance, then knock interrupts, camera snaps back to door. That's cinematic and uses the crowd. Then the letter slides under the door. Then the final peep. Good. Movement could stay locked the whole time; simpler and keeps focus. Intro is the only walking segment plus party.

The "non scary at home" intro: make it super cozy and mundane. A calendar, a potted plant, a TV playing a bad cooking show (static-ish screen with text?), a pizza box, a cat? A cat would be great. Add a low-poly cat on the couch that meows; if anomaly enters, cat runs away. The cat is a nice detail. Could be a simple box cat with ears and tail, idle bob. Interactable? "pet cat" mini-action that does nothing but is wholesome before the horror. Add a prompt "E — pet cat" maybe conflicts with letter prompt. Multiple interactables with nearest. Might be overkill but adds charm. Let's include a cat you can pet (with purr synth) and a TV you can toggle. Hmm, time. Maybe a cat mesh without interaction but looking at you. Keep scope.

Audio plan (WebAudio):
- Master gain, compressor.
- Ambience: low drone (sine 55Hz) + TV static (noise buffer loop, lowpass) + occasional creak.
- Knock: three knocks with filtered noise/impulse.
- Door open creak: sawtooth pitch sweep + noise.
- Footsteps: low thump on walk.
- Human chatter: short formant blips per line? Subtitles carry.
- Party music: sequencer with square/triangle bass, kick, snare, hi-hat, cheesy melody. Tempo 118. Volume scales with guest count. A loop that starts when first guest arrives (quiet), full at party.
- Heartbeat when peeping anomaly? That would give it away. Better: ambient tension drone during peephole; if you knock an anomaly, a low growl.
- Jumpscare: loud distorted scream (noise + sawtooth cluster + pitch drop), sub boom, glass shatter. Then killing party music: detuned carnival loop? Use descending minor arpeggio + boom.
- Win: cheerful jingle.

Implement music carefully; it can make or break. WebAudio procedural music can sound bad in a good way. Let's write a simple scheduler with `setInterval`-ish lookahead using audioContext.currentTime. A 16-step loop with bass, lead, kick/snare. Start after user gesture. We can have "party level" parameter (0..1) controlling layers/tempo. At 50, go full. During killing, switch to horror mode.

Rendering details:
- Use WebGL (Three.js). Low-res: renderer.setSize(480, 270, false) and canvas CSS width/height 100%, image-rendering: pixelated. But aspect ratio: we need adapt to screen aspect. Use render target at fixed height 270 and width = round(270*aspect), then upscale. Or renderer setSize(canvas.clientWidth/scale, canvas.clientHeight/scale) with scale based on DPR. We want chunky pixels but not too chunky on mobile. Use a pixel scale target: internal width = min(640, clientWidth/2?) Let's do dynamic: renderScale = 3 on desktop (1440/3=480 wide), 2.5 on mobile (390/2.5=156 wide - too low). Better fixed internal height 300 and width according to aspect: 1440x900 -> 480x300; 390x844 -> 139x300 (very pixelated portrait). That's okay but the peephole face might be too blocky. Maybe internal height 360, width = aspect*360 => 166 wide on mobile, 576x360 desktop. Still chunky. On portrait mobile the world is narrow, which is fine but FOV vertical... Adjust FOV. Let's use internal height 320 and max width 720. On mobile, internal 320 high, 148 wide; UI is DOM so crisp. 3D peephole will be very pixelated in portrait — thematic. Might hinder inspection. Alternative: on mobile, use height 400 (170 wide). Hmm.

Actually use CSS pixelation with `image-rendering: pixelated` and render at 0.5 device resolution (e.g., 195x422 on iPhone). That's less extreme but still retro. Desktop 720x450 at 1440x900 -> 2x upscale. Visually good and chunky. Let's do pixelRatio target of ~0.5 of CSS pixels, capped internal width 800 and height 500. At desktop 1440x900 → 720x450. At mobile 390x844 → 195x422. That's fine. We can add a "scanline + grain + vignette" CSS overlay for texture.

- Post-processing: Use CSS filters? renderer canvas with image-rendering. Add overlay div with scanlines (repeating-linear-gradient), vignette (radial-gradient), grain (animated SVG noise or CSS). Also a subtle chromatic aberration only during glitch. Keep it.

- Lighting: Use ambient + point lights; MeshLambertMaterial mostly (cheap). Shadows: only the porch flashlight maybe. To keep shadows simple, use fake blob shadows (dark circles) under visitors and furniture. Add a moody spotlight porch light.

- Textures: generate canvas textures with a "painted" rough style. Use nearest filtering. Wallpaper: cream with faded floral pattern or stripes drawn cackhanded. Wood floor planks. Rug pattern. Door texture with panels. Picture frames with crude cat/family drawings. TV screen: animated static via canvas texture updated occasionally. Letter: paper texture with handwriting drawn on 3D plane? We can make the letter image in DOM overlay for readability, and a physical white rectangle on the floor.

- Visitor model: 
  - body: box torso, lower body/legs: two boxes, arms: boxes or cylinders, head: box with face texture on front (+Z). Hair: box/plane on top, hats.
  - Use canvas faces (128x128) with low-res drawing: skin background, eyes (white + pupil), brows, mouth, optional glasses, mustache. To make creepy, anomalies get extra eyes, huge grin, no eyes, etc. Faces uploaded as CanvasTexture, NearestFilter.
  - Human face variations with goofy expressions.
  - Faces on head front; if backwards tell, set head rotation y=PI and put a face on back too? For back-of-head tell, head faces away (texture on front not visible) — that's clear.
  - Scale variation, shirt colors. Add simple details: collar, buttons, belt.
  - Animations: idle sway (torso), breathing, occasional blink (swap texture? expensive). Could animate head tilt. For jumpscare, animate.

- Group: positions on porch side by side, facing door. Make sure they fit; porch width 6, so 3-5 people at x -1.6..1.6. 5 might overlap; offset z slightly.

Peephole view:
- Camera located just outside door at eye height (1.6), looking at visitor. Actually peephole is in the door; camera a few cm outside. FOV maybe 75 with fisheye distortion? Simulate fisheye by rendering with wide FOV and applying CSS `border-radius: 50%; transform: scale(1.1)`? The circular mask is CSS overlay. In-game render stays full screen but a huge black vignette with circular hole via CSS radial-gradient or an SVG mask. Add slight barrel distortion via CSS? Can't easily. Could render to a WebGL shader for barrel distortion; overkill. Use a CSS `filter`? no. We'll fake with a circular mask + blur at edges.
- The peephole frame: black overlay with a transparent circle; add glass glare. The HUD sits around it.
- Visitors visible through the hole. The camera can turn slightly. 
- When not peeping: normal view of door. Once peeped and stepped back, the visitor remains waiting (model still visible through? door is closed). Fine.

Interaction flow / UI states:
- `MODE_TITLE`, `MODE_INTRO`, `MODE_LETTER`, `MODE_DOOR_IDLE` (waiting for knock? actually knock immediately on entering), `MODE_KNOCK` (buttons peep/open), `MODE_PEEP`, `MODE_VERDICT` (auto after accept/reject?), `MODE_PARTY`, `MODE_FINAL`, `MODE_DEATH`, `MODE_WIN`.
- Knock cycle: `spawnVisitor()` creates group outside, plays knock, shows door UI. The player can peep, knock, flash, decide. 
- If they click "OPEN DOOR" without peeping: treat as accept and trigger outcome (brave/foolish). The door opens; camera stays; visitor enters. If anomaly, immediate killing. If human, +N. This is fair because button says "open".
- Accept: hide UI; door swings open (animate), visitors walk in (animate along path), camera pulls back slightly; light/confetti for humans; counter increments; after animation, door closes, next knock after ~1.5s.
- Reject: door stays closed; if human, they say disappointed line and walk away; if anomaly, it bangs and maybe scratches; then next knock.
- Anomaly accept: door opens, anomaly doesn't walk so much as glide in / head twitches; then screen glitch, door slams, red; killing party.
- At count >= 50 after accepting: instead of next knock, trigger party cutscene. Camera turns to room, dancing, lights, music; overlay "HOUSE PARTY". After 9s, knock; camera snaps to door, final letter (display a note overlay "one more." maybe), peep final anomaly. Actually the final visitor could be a "human-looking" one with a tell only visible if you look carefully — e.g., it's the same anomaly from the letter, very tall. If you keep out → win. If let in → death. If the player opens without peeping → death. Good.

Should the final knock come even if the player let anomalies in? They'd already be dead. Yes.

Winning:
- Win overlay: "YOU DID IT. 50 humans are in your house. The door is closed. Nothing bad happened. The party continues." + a bad review quote: "0/10 too much standing" — The Door Review. And "PLAY AGAIN".
- Maybe win screen shows the party behind with the closed door and the anomaly peering through the peephole. A final creepy frame: peephole lights up with an eye. Nice.

Death:
- Killing party sequence ~7s with jumpscares. Then death overlay: "YOU LET IT IN." / "KILLING PARTY" with stats: guests betrayed, time stood at door, anomalies incorrectly admitted: 1. Buttons "TRY AGAIN". Red/black.

Now, implementation complexity. We need to write robust code and test. Let's estimate ~1800 lines JS + 500 CSS + 150 HTML. That's a lot but doable. Use modules to keep organized:
- `js/audio.js` — AudioEngine.
- `js/textures.js` — procedural textures/faces.
- `js/visitors.js` — visitor model builder & tells.
- `js/world.js` — build room, porch, party crowd, lights, TV.
- `js/main.js` — game state, UI bindings, render loop.
Maybe `js/letter.js` not needed.

Let's start by scaffolding and vendoring three.

Note: using ES modules from file server requires correct MIME; default-start server handles .js. Good. Import paths relative.

Need to ensure no errors in capture. Also mobile. Playwright screenshot at 1s after auto-start. If title start leads into intro, screenshot will show intro scene. Good. We want the initial capture to look interesting: maybe start screen is more impressive. But auto-start clicks START, so screenshot shows the game intro. That's okay; make intro visually rich. Could make the "START" button lead to a short intro overlay? The capture screenshot is the game. We'll verify.

Copy both files.

Now let's write the code. I'll use a coherent design and be careful with state.

Detailed 3D scene layout:

Coordinate: room x ∈ [-5,5], z ∈ [-4.5, 4.5], y 0..3.2. Door on front wall z=-4.5, centered x=0, width 1.1, height 2.2. Porch outside z from -4.5 to -8, width 10. Camera start at (0, 1.62, 3.4) looking toward -z (door). Letter at (0.4, 0.02, -3.3)? Actually near door on mat at z=-3.7. We need to walk ~6m. That's fine, slow walk 3 m/s = 2s. Maybe start closer: (0,1.62,2.6). 

Room details:
- Floor: planks texture repeated, 10x9 plane.
- Ceiling: off-white.
- Walls: wallpaper texture, back wall at z=4.5, side walls at x=±5. Front wall z=-4.5 with door hole? We can just place a wall plane with door mesh in front; no actual hole needed since door is closed and peephole camera is outside. But when the door opens, we need to see the porch and opening. Build front wall as segments around the door (left, right, top) so there is an actual opening. Door mesh hinged at x=-0.55, rotates open around Y. Good.
- Door frame boxes.
- Doormat at z=-3.9.
- Couch at x=-2.8, z=1.4 facing +z? Let's place couch along left wall facing right/center: position (-3.5, 0, 0.8), rotation y=PI/2. TV on right wall? Better layout: couch at (0,0,2.8) facing -z toward TV? But then TV would be by the door. Let's do:
  - Couch at (-2.6, 0, 1.8), rotated to face +x (toward center). Back against left wall.
  - TV stand at (3.6, 0, 1.6) against right wall, TV facing -x.
  - Coffee table at (0.4, 0, 1.6), rug under.
  - Bookshelf at (-4.7, 0, -2.8) along left wall.
  - Kitchen counter at (4.2, 0, -2.6) along right wall with microwave.
  - Plant at (-4.4, 0, 3.8), another near door (3.8, 0, -3.4).
  - Cat on couch.
  - Framed pictures on back wall and side.
  - Ceiling lamp at (0,3.0,0.5): warm point light + shade.
  - Window on right wall? Not needed.
  - Door mat and a small side table with keys.
  - Balloons etc. spawn in party.

Lighting:
- Ambient 0.35 warm.
- Point light at ceiling (0, 2.8, 0.8), intensity 25 (with physicallyCorrect? Three r187 uses physically correct by default; point light intensity in candela; use high values. Use `renderer.useLegacyLights`? Removed. For PointLight, intensity ~20 with distance 12, decay 2. Let's test visually. Ambient/Hemisphere is easier. Use HemisphereLight warm/cool intensity 0.6, plus PointLight 15 distance 14, plus TV glow blue. We'll adjust from screenshots.
- Porch light: PointLight warm above door outside, intensity 8, distance 8.
- Moonlight: DirectionalLight bluish low intensity.
- Party: colored point lights.

Materials: MeshLambertMaterial. Note MeshLambert supports lights. Textures with colorSpace = SRGBColorSpace.

Texture generation helper: create canvas w/h, draw, return CanvasTexture with NearestFilter, RepeatWrapping, colorSpace. Need to keep texture references to dispose maybe not.

Textures:
- wallpaper: base #d9cbb0, vertical faint stripes, small flowers; grunge noise. Repeat 4x2 maybe. Use `repeat.set(2,1)`.
- wood floor: planks with grain lines, repeat 4x4.
- rug: concentric rectangles, fringe.
- door: vertical wood panels drawn.
- porch wood: darker planks.
- ceiling: plaster.
- TV: dynamic canvas 128x96 with static + "COOKING?" maybe. We can animate by redrawing every 100ms; CanvasTexture needsUpdate.
- letter, paintings, cat fur? Simple colors.
- Faces: 128x128; draw skin base with noise, eyes. For low-res crude quality, use 64x64. Pixelated and expressive. Human faces have varying features. Face texture applied to front face of head box? BoxGeometry material array: 6 materials. Simpler: head box with plain skin material, then a plane slightly in front with the face texture (transparent background). But transparent + low-res. Or material array with face on +Z index 4. BoxGeometry material order: +x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z. Use [skin, skin, hair?? no, hair as separate mesh, skin, faceMat, skin]. Face texture should include skin background so it blends. Good. But if head rotates, face moves correctly. Hair as a box cap + maybe back. Great.
- Faces need different skin tone; draw base accordingly.
- For anomalies, face texture with extra eyes etc.

Model builder:
```
function makePerson(opts) {
  const g = new THREE.Group();
  const scale = opts.height ?? 1;
  // legs: two boxes from y=0 to 0.85 (scaled)
  // torso: box 0.55 x 0.65 x 0.3 at y 1.15
  // arms: boxes 0.14x0.6x0.14 at ±0.36, y 1.2; pivot groups at shoulder to swing
  // head group at y=1.65; head box 0.42; face plane/material
  // hair etc.
}
```
Use normalized body height ~1.75 * heightScale. Tells:
- tall: whole group scale 1.25 (head near top). Porch light height fixed; camera look at face maybe. If too tall, head may be cut off. Use 1.18 max.
- long neck: head group y +0.35, plus a thin neck box.
- extra arms: add 1-2 arms at lower/upper positions; animate.
- extra eyes: face texture.
- no face: blank skin.
- wide mouth: face.
- backwards: head rotation y=PI (face hidden, hair/back of head visible). Add hair back patch.
- float: group y = 0.18 and no shadow; sway.
- duplicate: add a second person behind (simplified clone) at z-0.8, slightly offset, same face/colors. Creepy.
- skin: green/grey/pale.
- long fingers: add thin boxes at hands.
- twitch: animate rotations.
- they breathe/sway.

I want visitors to read well through the peephole. Place visitors at z=-6.2, camera at z=-4.42 (just outside door). Distance 1.8m. FOV 70. A 1.75m person at 1.8m distance fills ~ 55° vertical; fine. Camera eye 1.6, visitor head 1.6. Good. For tall, head at 2.1; still visible. Group of 4 side by side at x offsets -1.5..1.5; with FOV 70 and distance 1.8, horizontal half-width visible ~1.26m at that plane, so 3 max. Move group further to z=-7 and spread 2.6. FOV horizontal depends on aspect. For 16:9, hFOV ~ 100°, half width at 2.6m ~ 3.1m. Portrait, hFOV is much smaller (FOV is vertical; at 390x844, vertical FOV 70, horizontal ~37°, half width 0.88 at 2.6) — crowds won't fit on mobile. Hmm. Need responsive FOV and group layout. For portrait, use wider vertical? Set camera FOV depending on aspect: if aspect < 1, use FOV 85 and move camera/visitors? Better: group positions based on available horizontal FOV. Compute halfWidth = tan(hFOV/2)*dist. Place group within ±0.75*halfWidth. On portrait, they'd be tightly packed; maybe scale down the group (further back) by moving z to -8.5 and lower camera? Or render peephole as a full circle that crops. Maybe put group at z=-7.5 (3m away), fitting 3 people in portrait (half width ~1.0 at 3m, so 2m width). 4 people at 0.5 spacing = 2m. Use smaller spacing (0.5) and overlap slightly, okay. But detail at 3m is smaller. Pixelated 200px wide, still okay with zoom.

We can add a "ZOOM" (hold or toggle) that reduces FOV to 35, letting you scan faces. The player can pan left/right. This solves mobile. With zoom, you see detail and can scan across group. Let's implement zoom toggle `Z`/button. In peephole, camera yaw can pan ±20° and pitch ±10°; zoom FOV 38. Actually simpler: default FOV 60, zoom FOV 32, mouse/pointer pans look. The zoom button is important for tells. HUD hint "ZOOM Z".

Visitor arrangement: positions x centered. For groups, maybe arrange in a slight arc. Camera at door center. Default view shows all. Good.

Anomaly detection UI: maybe a stamp/book? After peeping, verdict buttons. Add "WHO IS IT?" ask button (A) that shows a subtitle line and triggers a reaction; can reveal voice. Could combine with knock. Let's have "KNOCK" button; humans respond confused, anomalies twitch. Add subtitle speech. Maybe "ASK" = same. Keep one.

Group interaction: subtitles from one member. Humans have names & lines:
- "hi! i brought ice."
- "is this the party?"
- "we brought chips."
- "hello, i am a normal human."
- "your lawn is on fire."
- "sorry we're late."
- "i love your door."
Random funny lines, slightly off. Anomaly lines:
- "let me in. i am human."
- "i have skin."
- "i brought 50 friends." (only one figure)
- "it is cold out here. i have too many arms."
- "hello i am your neighbor (lie)."
- "the door is nice. i will eat it."
- "knock knock. i am not a monster." 
- subtitle should maybe not reveal type too obviously unless audio/voice weird. Lines like "i have skin" make it obvious. That's fine for comedy; but tells should be visual. Keep anomaly lines slightly suspicious but not definitive: "i am human. i am human. i am human." or "you have nice skin." Human lines normal. This adds another layer. But we don't want text to trivialize. Maybe after knocking (reaction) the anomaly says weird lines; so using the knock action gives info. Good: initial ask returns "hi." / silence. Knock reaction reveals.

For audio voices: use WebAudio "speech" grunts (short filtered saw with pitch envelope) with subtitle. Humans: two-tone friendly. Anomalies: detuned low growl. If you use the ask/knock, the voice is a tell. But subtitles already tell; make anomaly subtitles weird but ambiguous. Fine.

Flow specifics:
- On knock: door UI "Someone is at the door." Buttons: [PEEP] [OPEN DOOR]. Maybe show a "knock" indicator animation. Press PEEP → animate camera to peephole. Show visitor(s).
- In peephole: top-left shows guest count. Lower panel with buttons: [FLASHLIGHT] [KNOCK] [ZOOM] [LET IN] [KEEP OUT]. Plus a hint "look for tells: eyes, arms, shadow, height, face".
- The first peep triggers a tutorial overlay with 3 tips, dismiss with "OK". Maybe avoid blocking; show a small note.
- LET IN => outcome.
- KEEP OUT => outcome.
- After outcome, step back automatically to door, close door; 1.2s later next knock. Guest count animates.
- There is no timer, so players can inspect.

Game length concern: 50 guests with avg group 3 = 17 accepts. Anomaly rate 30% means ~7 rejects. 24 peeps. If each takes 8-15s, 4-6 min. Fine.

Difficulty ramp: Anomaly probability 0.25 + min(0.2, guests/50*0.2). Early obvious, later subtler. Ensure no two anomalies in a row? Random. Avoid too many humans after 50? Final separate.

Tells selection by difficulty:
- Early (guests<15): from strong tells [extraEyes, extraArms, tall, noFace, float, duplicate, backwards].
- Later: chance strong 0.6, subtle 0.4 [skin, fingers, twitch, wrongShadow, longNeck].
But "wrongShadow" requires flashlight. The flashlight toggle is available, so okay. Could be too subtle if they never use flashlight. Add a checklist hint "shadow" in the tutorial. And a "flashlight" button. Fine.
- To be fair, every anomaly should have at least one tell visible without flashlight or revealed via knock. For subtle-only anomalies, knock reaction triggers twitch. Good.
- Final anomaly: tall + extra eyes + wrong shadow; obvious enough but unnerving.

Stats and HUD:
- Guests count with a party bar and tiny person icons? Use text "GUESTS 12 / 50" and a bar.
- Rejected human count? "TURNED AWAY 3" maybe. It could be used for an ending evaluation, but not fail.
- Objective text changes.
- A "night" indicator "NIGHT 1" and a clock that advances absurdly with each guest (7:00 PM → 3:00 AM) for flavor.
- "VIBES" meter maybe. Skip.

Intro walk:
- Pointer lock: clicking canvas requests lock. But on title screen button click, no lock. In intro, the user can look by moving mouse without pointer lock when pointer is over canvas? Best: implement drag-look always, plus pointer lock on click. For desktop, clicking canvas locks pointer. Show hint. For mobile, touch drag to look and joystick to move.
- Since the capture only screenshots, not critical, but functionality must be real.
- We should support keyboard-only too: WASD + arrow look? Add Q/E? Interact E. Arrow keys rotate. Good accessibility.
- Mobile joystick: left thumb area, drag. Action button "E" appears when near letter. The letter interaction on mobile via button. Screen drag look.
- Since we don't know if they will play on mobile, implement solid basic controls.

Maybe simplify intro walking by auto-walking? No, the walking segment adds immersion. But a "bad quality" game can have janky controls. Still make them work.

Player collision: clamp x to [-4.4,4.4], z to [-4.0,4.1]; avoid furniture via simple AABBs? We can let player walk through furniture (funny and low quality), or add collision. A few boxes. Might be fine to just clamp room and allow through coffee table. To keep smooth, add collision circles for couch and table. Eh, implement simple AABB push-out for main furniture, or skip. I'd skip except walls/door: collision with door wall z>-4.0. Player can't go through door anyway since locked at door phase. In intro, clamp z > -4.0.

Camera control at door: player position fixed (0,1.62,-2.9) facing door; mouse look yaw/pitch (clamp yaw ±80°? To see party behind, allow ±180°? At the door, if you look back, you see the party. Allow full yaw. Pitch clamp ±60. Use pointer lock / drag. The peephole view is a separate camera position with its own yaw/pitch clamp around straight ahead.

Door view: The peephole is at y=1.55 on the door. When peeping, the main camera moves to (0,1.55,-4.52) outside looking at -z; FOV 65. The door is behind the camera (not visible). The peephole overlay circle. The porch and visitor visible. When stepping back, camera returns to door position.

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable browser horror game matching the user's premise: a "bad quality" (intentionally janky) horror game where you're safe at home, receive a letter saying "stand at the door", inspect visitors through a peephole, let in 50 humans to trigger a house party, and if you let in a non-human anomaly, trigger a "killing party" with jumpscares and death.
- Build request stated: "Build a complete, playable game now... Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish."

## Requirements
- Game must be fully playable, not a demo.
- Story beats required: normal home intro → letter → stand at door → judge human vs non-human → 50 humans = house party → anomaly admitted = killing party/jumpscares/death.
- Intentional low-quality / ugly aesthetic is desired, but gameplay must be coherent and functional.
- Must support desktop and mobile/touch (per repo conventions in AGENTS.md, which the next agent receives separately).
- Static deployment with `index.html` at repo root; no package.json at root (would trigger unsupported project detection).
- Do not ask clarifying questions.

## Decisions
- Built as vanilla ES modules + Three.js, fully vendored locally (no CDN):
  - `vendor/three.module.js` + `vendor/three.core.js` copied from `three@0.187.0`.
  - Procedural canvas textures and hand-drawn faces; no external image assets.
- Web Audio API for all sound/music (synth party loop, knocks, screams, jumpscare stingers).
- Low-res internal renderer (~52–58% of screen) upscaled with `image-rendering: pixelated`, plus scanlines/grain/vignette for PS1/jank vibe.
- Game structure:
  - Title screen → walkable living-room intro → letter overlay → door/peephole loop → house party at 50 → final "tall one" visitor → win or killing party.
  - Peephole shows 1–4 visitors; LET IN / KEEP OUT; flashlight (F), knock reaction (K), zoom (Z), step back (Esc).
  - Anomaly tells: extra eyes, extra arms, tall, no face, backwards head, floating, duplicate, long neck, weird skin, long fingers, twitch, no shadow, mismatched eyes. Anomalies are solo; humans arrive in groups of 1–4.
  - Rejecting a human loses no life but wastes a visit; rejecting an anomaly is safe; admitting an anomaly triggers the killing party.
  - Final round is a forced tall + 3-eyed + no-shadow anomaly; rejecting wins, admitting dies.
- Debug hooks exposed as `window.__GAME`: `intro()`, `letter()`, `peep(kind, tell)`, `final()`, `party()`, `death()`, `win()`, `accept()`, `reject()`, `setGuests(n)`, `info()`.
- Vendored Google Fonts locally: Bungee, Patrick Hand, Special Elite, with OFL license files.
- Start screen `START` button matches capture auto-start regex.

## Work State

### Completed
- `index.html` — full UI shell: canvas, HUD, title screen, letter overlay, door UI, peephole UI, party banner, jumpscare layer, ending screen, mobile controls.
- `css/style.css` — complete responsive styling, paper-note HUD, peephole circular mask, animations, mobile layout, safe-area handling.
- `js/textures.js` — procedural wallpaper/floor/rug/door/porch/ceiling/doormat/TV/paintings/banner/sign/star textures; hand-drawn face generation, human/anomaly face specs.
- `js/visitors.js` — low-poly human/anomaly model builder, all anomaly tells, idle/dance/death animations, gross faces, lines/reactions.
- `js/world.js` — house interior, porch, door, furniture, cat, TV, lights, party decor, confetti, crowd/visitor groups, door animation.
- `js/audio.js` — AudioEngine with procedural ambience, party music, horror mode, knocks, door creak/slam, footsteps, voices, screams, jingles, mute.
- `js/main.js` — initial full assembly: state machine, intro movement, letter flow, rounds, peephole, decisions, crowd walk-in, house party, killing party, endings, camera tweens, input, mobile joystick, debug hooks, boot loop.

### Active
- Integration/verification has not yet been run at all — no server started, no browser load, no screenshot, no JS console check yet.

The `const` is in the TDZ, but functions only execute after boot, so it may be fine; still verify.

6. Add a concise README note / final response with assumptions (intentional jank, procedural assets, debug hooks).
7. Confirm the final static build works with the repo's default start path (root `index.html`, no package.json).
